title: Two Banquets and a Walk on the Sea
summary: Herod Antipas, hearing of Jesus, fears that John the Baptist has come back to life, and Matthew tells how Herod had John beheaded at a birthday feast. Jesus withdraws, has compassion on the crowds, and feeds five thousand men, besides women and children, from five loaves and two fish. That night he walks on the sea to his disciples, Peter walks toward him and begins to sink, and those in the boat worship him as the Son of God.
story: Chapter 13 ended with Jesus rejected in his hometown. Chapter 14 shows a more dangerous rejection: the ruler of Galilee has already killed the prophet who prepared Jesus' way. From here to chapter 17, Jesus often withdraws from public places and gives more attention to forming his disciples, and the Gospel moves toward Peter's confession in chapter 16. This chapter sets two banquets side by side. At Herod's table there is luxury, a rash oath, and a prophet's death. In the wilderness, at Jesus' table, there is bread for the hungry and baskets left over. The night on the sea then brings the disciples, for the first time in Matthew, to worship Jesus as the Son of God.
historical:
Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas, who ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. Matthew also calls him king in verse 9, as people commonly did, though Rome never granted him that title. He had divorced his first wife, a daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas IV, to marry Herodias, a granddaughter of Herod the Great and the wife of his half-brother. Marrying a brother's wife while the brother lived was forbidden by Leviticus 18:16 and 20:21, which is John's objection in verse 4. The Gospels call Herodias's first husband Philip, while Josephus calls him simply Herod; many historians think he bore both names, and he is distinct from Philip the tetrarch who ruled the region northeast of the lake.

Josephus also recounts John's death, placing his imprisonment at the fortress of Machaerus east of the Dead Sea and saying that Antipas feared John's influence might lead to revolt. He names Herodias's daughter as Salome and adds that when Aretas later defeated Antipas in battle, around AD 36, some Jews saw it as God's judgment for the killing of John. The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle of Jesus' ministry told in all four Gospels (Mark 6:30-44, Luke 9:10-17, John 6:1-15). The walk on the sea appears also in Mark 6 and John 6, but only Matthew tells of Peter's steps on the water. Gennesaret (verse 34) was a fertile plain on the northwest shore of the lake.
cultural:
Royal birthday banquets were occasions for display, and dancing by a young woman of the royal family before male guests would have been seen as scandalous by many Jews. An oath sworn before guests put a ruler's honor at stake, and Herod is trapped more by his fear of shame than by any sense of right. Beheading was a Roman form of execution.

In the wilderness scene, Jesus follows the pattern of a Jewish meal: he takes the bread, looks up to heaven, speaks a blessing to God, breaks it, and gives it. The twelve baskets (kophinos, a sturdy wicker basket) hold far more than the meal began with. Counting only the men, as verse 21 does, was a common way of reckoning crowds, and Matthew alone adds that women and children were there as well, so the crowd was considerably larger. The night was divided by Romans into four watches, and the fourth ran from about three to six in the morning. Fishermen feared the sea at night, and ancient people commonly believed that spirits of the dead could appear, which explains the disciples' cry that they were seeing a ghost.
literary: The chapter opens with a flashback (verses 3 to 12), one of the few extended stories in Matthew in which Jesus does not appear. Its placement sets up the contrast of two rulers and two feasts. The feeding and the sea crossing then form a pair also found in Mark and John, suggesting the two events were linked in early tradition. Matthew's feeding account closely echoes the wording of the Last Supper in 26:26: taking, blessing, breaking, and giving bread. The sea story mirrors the storm in 8:23-27, but moves further. There the disciples asked what kind of man this was; here they answer the question by worshiping him as the Son of God. Peter's walk (verses 28 to 31) is a small drama of faith and fear, and it prepares for Peter's larger role in chapters 16 and 17.

outline.t: Herod fears that John has risen
The death of John the Baptist
Five thousand fed in a desolate place
Peter on the water; the disciples worship

doctrines.note: Jesus feeds his people in the wilderness as God fed Israel with manna, walks on the sea as only God does in Job 9:8, and speaks words that echo God's self-naming. The disciples' confession that he is truly the Son of God is Matthew's answer to who he is.

Peter's walk shows faith as trust in Jesus' word (“Come”) and doubt as attention turning from Jesus to the wind. Even sinking, Peter prays the shortest of prayers, and Jesus immediately reaches out his hand.

The feeding shows God's provision through Jesus, working with what is given, however little. The disciples are told to give the crowd something to eat themselves, and the bread passes through their hands to the people.

words.note: Ego, I. In verse 27 Jesus says literally ego eimi, I am, which in context means it is I. But the same words are used in the Greek Old Testament where God names himself (as in Exodus 3:14 and Isaiah 43:10), and spoken by one who walks on the sea they carry more than simple identification.

Distazo, to doubt or waver, literally to stand in two ways. It appears in the New Testament only here and in 28:17, where some of the disciples doubt even as they worship the risen Jesus. It describes a divided mind in a person who has faith, not the settled refusal of unbelief.

Chortazo, to feed until full or to satisfy. Originally used of fattening animals with fodder, it came to mean eating one's fill. Everyone ate and was satisfied, echoing God's promises to satisfy the hungry (as in Psalm 107:9) and Jesus' blessing on those who hunger and thirst for righteousness in 5:6.

Eulogeo, to bless, literally to speak well. In Jewish practice the blessing at a meal was spoken to God, praising him as the giver of bread. Jesus' blessing in verse 19 is thanksgiving to the Father, the same act he will perform over bread at the Last Supper (26:26).

christ: The chapter sets Jesus against the backdrop of Israel's story. As God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness, Jesus feeds a multitude in a desolate place, and the leftover baskets point to abundance rather than bare survival. Psalm 23 pictured the Lord as a shepherd who makes his flock lie down in green pastures and spreads a table for them; here Jesus has the crowd sit on the grass and feeds them. The Old Testament describes God as the one who treads on the waves of the sea (Job 9:8) and makes a path through the mighty waters (Isaiah 43:16), and Jesus walks on the sea to his frightened followers. The contrast with Herod is pointed: the false king feasts and kills the prophet, while the true king, himself soon to be killed by rulers, feeds the hungry and saves the sinking. The meal's words, taking, blessing, breaking, and giving, anticipate the bread of the Last Supper and his body given for many.

hard.q: Did Jesus really multiply bread and walk on water, or are these stories meant to be read symbolically?
hard.a: Modern readers often find nature miracles harder to accept than healings. Some nineteenth-century rationalist interpreters proposed natural explanations, for example that the crowd shared food they had brought, or that Jesus was walking on the shore or in shallows. Many later scholars have read the stories as symbolic narratives, created or shaped by early Christians to express faith in Jesus through Old Testament images of manna and God's power over the sea. The Gospel writers themselves narrate these events as things that happened, witnessed by the disciples, and the feeding is attested in all four Gospels, including John, who writes independently of the others. Historic Christian faith has received them as real acts of God, arising from the conviction that God acted in Jesus and raised him from the dead, which makes lesser miracles unsurprising. The symbolic meaning and the historical claim need not compete: the stories carry rich Old Testament echoes precisely because, on the Gospels' own account, the God of the exodus was acting again in Jesus. Readers will weigh the question according to their convictions about whether God acts in the world at all.

questions: Herod did wrong to protect his image before his guests. Where does fear of what others think push you toward choices you know are wrong?
The disciples saw five loaves and a crowd, and Jesus said, “Bring them here to Me.” What small thing might you be holding back from him?
Peter's faith faltered when he looked at the wind. What winds pull your attention away from Jesus, and what helps you look back?
